newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia pay TV battle claims Optus CEO.
newsitem.headline: Australia pay TV battle claims Optus CEO.

text.p: An expensive battle between Australia's two largest telecommunications groups for control of pay television claimed its first major victim on Friday when Optus Communications chief executive Ziggy Switkowski resigned.
Optus, Australia's second biggest telecommunications carrier, said Ziggy Switkowski had tendered his resignation and would be replaced by Briton Peter Howell-Davies.
Optus also said chairman Russell Fynmore had resigned.
Switkowski became chief executive about one year ago after a long career at Eastman Kodak Co. His resignation had been mooted for a number of weeks.
Newspapers have reported that the Optus board was unhappy with Switkowski's handling of some strategic issues, in particular the future of the pay-television unit Optus Vision.
The statement by Optus did not say why Switkowski had resigned but said one of Howell-Davies' first duties would be to focus on Optus Vision.
"My first task will be to work directly with the shareholders to ensure that Optus Vision is handled in an expeditious way that protects and enhances this position," Howell-Davies said.
Howell-Davies was a director of Optus from 1993-95 and since then has been chief executive of Mercury Communications, a unit of London's Cable and Wireless Plc.
Cable and Wireless has a 24.5-percent stake in Optus, the same as that held by BellSouth Corp of the United States.
Local transport and health care group Mayne Nickless Ltd is the largest shareholder with a 24.9-percent stake.
Mayne Nickless welcomed the leadership change and said that continuing problems at Optus Vision meant the float of Optus Communiciations was uncertain.
The Optus float had previously been planned for the end of 1997.

The Australian telecommunications industry will be fully deregulated from July 1 this year, which means Optus can compete in all markets with state-owned carrier Telstra Corp -- Australia's largest telecoms group.

Telstra is expected to be privatised by the end of 1997, but is bedevilled by legal action by competitors and huge losses from Foxtel, its cable television joint venture with Rupert Murdoch's News Corp.
Optus Vision, which has about 185,000 subscribers, is involved in a fierce battle for market share with Foxtel, which has about 140,000 subscribers.
The two pay-TV groups, and the struggling third-ranked Australis Media Ltd, are estimated to have lost a combined A$1.5 billion (US$1.13 billion).
Foxtel has committed to spending A$3 billion on cabling as many households as possible in Australian cities, but is looking at cutting that rollout short to save money.
Australis said earlier on Friday that it was involved in possible merger talks with either Optus Vision or Foxtel.

A merger of Foxtel and Australis was blocked by anti-monopolies regulators in late 1995 but Australis sources said they were more confident now that a merger would not be blocked due to upcoming telecoms deregulation.
